note_claims.claim: The presenting complaint is a first seizure occurring 3 months ago.
The seizure involved going quiet, followed by left arm jerking for a few seconds, generalized stiffening, and shaking.
The shaking lasted about 2 minutes (confirmed by the clock).
Associated symptoms included perioral cyanosis, lateral tongue bite, and urinary incontinence.
The patient experienced post-ictal confusion lasting about 20 minutes.
The seizure was preceded by sleep deprivation after four consecutive night shifts.
The patient reported no alcohol consumption that day.
The patient reported no recreational drug use.
The patient has no previous history of seizures, myoclonic jerks, or absences.
The patient has no history of head injury or CNS infection.
The patient has no family history of epilepsy.
The patient works as a warehouse supervisor.
The patient reports no regular medications.
The patient reports no known drug allergies.
The neurological examination was normal.
The CT scan in A&E was normal.
The blood tests were normal.
The impression is a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure, possibly of focal onset (left arm, suggesting right hemisphere), provoked in part by sleep deprivation.
The plan includes an MRI brain scan using an epilepsy protocol and an EEG.
No antiseizure medication is prescribed at present.
Safety advice includes using showers instead of baths, avoiding swimming alone, avoiding heights, and maintaining a regular sleep pattern.
A clinic review with results is scheduled in about six weeks.
If a further seizure occurs, the patient should put him in the recovery position, time it, and call 999 if it lasts more than five minutes or if he is injured.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician is Dr Iyer from the first seizure clinic.
Relative is Bethany, the patient's wife.
Patient recalls nothing specific about the event, stating he was watching telly and paramedics arrived.
The event occurred three weeks ago on a Sunday night.
Relative describes the event: he went quiet, then his left arm started jerking for a few seconds, followed by generalized stiffening and shaking.
Relative initially estimated the shaking lasted five minutes, but confirmed it lasted two minutes when checking the clock.
Relative reports the patient's lips went a bit blue, he bit his tongue on the side, and he wet himself.
The patient was confused for about twenty minutes afterwards.
Patient reports having done four night shifts in a row and had maybe four hours' sleep.
Patient reports having no alcohol that day, stating he only has a few pints at the weekend.
Patient reports no recreational drug use.
Patient reports no previous history of funny turns, jerks in the morning, or blank spells.
Patient reports no history of head injuries or meningitis as a child.
Patient reports no family history of epilepsy.
Patient reports no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
Patient confirms he drives to work.
Clinician states the neurological examination is completely normal today.
Clinician states the CT scan in A&E was normal.
Clinician states the blood tests were normal.
Clinician suggests the event sounds like a seizure, possibly of focal onset (left arm, suggesting right hemisphere), provoked in part by lack of sleep.
Clinician suggests an MRI scan of the brain using an epilepsy protocol and an EEG.
Clinician states that no tablets are usually needed after a first seizure and they will decide once results are available.
Clinician advises that by law, the patient must not drive and needs to tell the DVLA about the seizure.
Clinician advises the patient not to drive in the meantime and suggests the employer may help with shifts.
Clinician provides safety tips: have showers, not baths; don't swim alone; and avoid heights.
Clinician explains seizure first aid to the wife: put him on his side, time it, and call 999 if it lasts more than five minutes or if he is injured.
Clinician states the patient will see them in the clinic with the results in about six weeks.

findings.note_span: The presenting complaint is a first seizure 3 months ago.
findings.transcript_evidence: Three weeks ago, on the Sunday night.
findings.rationale: The note incorrectly states the seizure occurred 3 months ago when the transcript indicates it occurred 3 weeks ago, which is a significant temporal error.
